text:
Every database query starts with the same question: where is the data? Without an index, the database has to read every row in the table, one after another, until it finds what you asked for. You'd never notice on a small table. On a big one, it's why your dashboard spins and your users leave.

An index works like the one at the back of a textbook. It's a separate, sorted structure, usually a B-tree, that maps the values you search on to where the matching rows live. A B-tree stays balanced and branches widely at every level, so finding a value takes O(log n) steps instead of n. Even with millions of rows, the database visits only a handful of nodes to reach the right one.

In one case, a query against a 10-million-row table dropped from 2.1 seconds to 4 milliseconds once the right index was in place.

Indexes do cost something, though. Every insert, update, and delete now has to maintain the index as well, which slowed writes by about 15%. The hard part is knowing when that trade-off is worth it.
